interactions.label: If the lateral pectoral nerve is damaged during axillary surgery, which specific

params.question: If the lateral pectoral nerve is damaged during axillary surgery, which specific action of pectoralis major would be most affected?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adduction involves both the clavicular and sternocostal heads, so it would be partly preserved by the intact sternocostal head supplied by the medial pectoral nerve.

answers.text: Flexion of the arm at the shoulder

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6, C7) specifically supplies the clavicular head, which is responsible for flexion of the arm at the shoulder up to 90 degrees.
Extension from a flexed position is the action of the sternocostal head, primarily supplied by the medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1), which remains intact in this scenario.
Medial rotation is contributed to by both heads of the muscle, so it would only be partly weakened — not the most affected action.

overallFeedback.feedback: The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6, C7) specifically supplies the clavicular head of pectoralis major. The clavicular head's unique action is flexion of the arm at the shoulder, distinguishing it from the sternocostal head which handles extension from a flexed position.

Well done! The lateral pectoral nerve supplies the clavicular head, whose primary unique action is flexion of the arm at the shoulder. Damage spares the sternocostal actions but impairs forward flexion.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Level II axillary lymph nodes actually lie posterior to (behind) pectoralis minor, not lateral. The three levels are: Level I = lateral, Level II = posterior, Level III = medial to pectoralis minor.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. Level II axillary lymph nodes lie posterior to (behind) pectoralis minor, not lateral. Remember the three levels: Level I = lateral, Level II = posterior, Level III = medial to pectoralis minor.

interactions.label: A patient presents with a hard breast lump and visible skin dimpling over it. Wh

params.question: A patient presents with a hard breast lump and visible skin dimpling over it. Which structural mechanism best explains this clinical sign?

answers.text: Oedema of the subcutaneous fat causes uneven swelling of the skin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subcutaneous oedema would cause diffuse skin swelling, not the focal inward retraction characteristic of dimpling.

answers.text: The tumour compresses the lactiferous ducts, pulling the nipple inward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Compression of lactiferous ducts may lead to nipple retraction or discharge — a separate clinical sign from skin dimpling over the lump.

answers.text: Tumour invasion shortens Cooper's ligaments, pulling the overlying skin inward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cooper's ligaments (suspensory ligaments of the breast) connect the skin to the deep fascia. Tumour infiltration shortens these fibrous strands, pulling the overlying skin inward to produce the dimple sign.

answers.text: Venous obstruction by the tumour causes localised skin retraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Venous obstruction can cause superficial venous dilation, not the inward skin retraction characteristic of dimpling. Dimpling specifically results from Cooper's ligament shortening.

overallFeedback.feedback: Skin dimpling in breast cancer is caused by tumour invasion of Cooper's ligaments — the suspensory ligaments of the breast. These fibrous strands connect the skin to the deep fascia, and when a tumour shortens them, the overlying skin is pulled inward, producing the dimple sign.

Correct! Cooper's ligaments are fibrous strands running from the skin to the deep fascia. Their infiltration and shortening by a tumour creates the classic skin dimpling — one of the key signs of breast malignancy.

interactions.label: A newborn is found to have accessory breast tissue (polymastia) below the normal

params.question: A newborn is found to have accessory breast tissue (polymastia) below the normal left breast. Which embryological structure explains why such anomalies occur along a specific line on the body?

answers.text: The mammary ridge (milk line), an ectodermal thickening running from the axilla to the groin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The mammary ridge appears in the sixth week of embryonic development and normally regresses except at the fourth intercostal space. Polymastia results from incomplete regression of this ridge.

answers.text: The thoracic dermatomes, which guide segmental breast tissue distribution

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dermatomes reflect segmental sensory innervation of the skin. They do not guide breast tissue distribution, which is determined embryologically by the ectodermal mammary ridge.

answers.text: The pectoral fascia, which extends caudally along the anterior chest wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pectoral fascia is a connective tissue layer overlying pectoralis major. It does not determine breast tissue location — that is set embryologically by the mammary ridge.

answers.text: The lateral plate mesoderm, which forms the anterior body wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body wall musculature, but the breast is an ectodermal derivative — a modified sweat gland whose location is determined by the mammary ridge.

overallFeedback.feedback: Polymastia results from incomplete regression of the mammary ridge (milk line) — an ectodermal thickening appearing in the sixth week, running from the axilla to the groin. This embryological origin is why accessory breast tissue always appears along this specific line.

Well done! The mammary ridge runs from the axilla to the groin in the embryo. Its incomplete regression produces accessory breast tissue (polymastia) or nipples (polythelia) always along this line. Such tissue can potentially develop cancer and may lactate.
